# RESY

<!-- badges: start -->
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/RESY)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RESY)
[![CRAN checks](https://badges.cranchecks.info/worst/RESY.svg)](https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_RESY.html)
[![Downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/RESY?color=brightgreen)](https://www.r-pkg.org/pkg/RESY)
[![Dependencies](https://tinyverse.netlify.app/badge/RESY)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RESY)
<!-- badges: end -->

**RESY assigns vegetation plots to vegetation or habitat types based on their plant community.** A plot where beech, silver fir and beech-forest herbs such as
wood sorrel grow together is a beech-fir montane forest. A plot where mat-grass
(*Nardus stricta*) is abundant is an acidic grassland. RESY uses the species
composition and cover or abundance recorded in each vegetation plot (relevé).

The **rules** for this assignment **form an expert system** (ESy; Chytrý et al.
([2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)), stored as a text or JSON file. For
each type, the rule specifies which groups of indicator species a plot must
contain and how much cover they must have. In the example below, a plot is a
beech-fir montane forest when beech and silver fir together cover more than 15%
of it and beech-forest herbs more than 10%. You can also supply your own expert
system.

RESY ships the expert system of Chytrý et al. ([2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519))
for EUNIS (European Nature Information System), the habitat classification of
the European Environment Agency for the land and sea of Europe ([EUNIS habitats](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/123d0c9a-a6fa-4f2d-b887-5d8e5468faed)).
EUNIS defines a habitat by its plant and animal communities together with
abiotic conditions. Some of its rules therefore also use site data, such as the
ecoregion, the country or the position on the coast. With `resy_harmonize_eunis()`
you can  get such [additional information](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/EUNIS.html). Afterwards you can [apply an expert system](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/RESY.html) with `resy_classify()` to your vegetation relevés. 

Each expert system uses its own list of species names. The EUNIS expert system,
for example, uses the names of [Euro+Med PlantBase](https://europlusmed.org/),
the taxonomy used in data from the [European Vegetation Archive (EVA)](https://euroveg.org/eva-database/). Species names in plot data that follow another taxonomy, such as [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/)
or [World Flora Online](https://www.worldfloraonline.org/), must first be
matched to the names of the expert system. `resy_resolve_taxa()` does this for
any expert system: it removes author names and looks up synonyms. The synonym
table that comes with RESY links about 65,000 synonyms from six taxonomies
(Euro+Med, World Flora Online, GBIF, Catalogue of Life, ITIS and NCBI) to the
species names of the EUNIS expert system. For an expert system with other
species names, you can supply your own synonym table, as shown in
[Match species names](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/taxonomy.html).

The [RESY App](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/app.html) runs
RESY in your browser, without installing R. It classifies the example plots or
your own files with EUNIS-ESy or your own expert system, and shows the rules
behind each assignment.

## :arrow_double_down: Installation

The package is available on CRAN. Install and load it with:

``` r
install.packages("RESY")
library(RESY)
```

RESY is still under active development. You can install the development
version from the GitHub repository using the following commands:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
   "https://github.com/florian-jansen/resy",
   dependencies = TRUE
   )
library(RESY)
```

## :rocket: Usage

To classify plots, `resy_classify()` needs two tables:

- A **species table**, with one row per species in each plot, giving the plot
  ID, species name and cover.
- A **header table**, with one row per plot, giving the plot ID and any site
  data used by the classification rules.

This example uses the bundled plots from Tuscany and `Apennine-test`, a small
expert system whose rules require no site data. The header table therefore
contains only plot IDs, but `resy_classify()` still requires it.

```{r usage, message = FALSE}
library(RESY)

file <- system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY")
species <- read.csv(file)
header <- unique(species["PlotObservationID"])

res <- resy_classify(species, header, scheme = "Apennine-test")
cand <- resy_candidates(res, top_n = 3)
table(cand$classification)
```

`F`, `FB`, `N`, `NG` and `NS` are the five vegetation types of `Apennine-test`.
A plot marked `?` meets no type's rule and is not classified. Here, 92 of the
200 plots remain unclassified. In these plots, all four indicator groups have at
most 4% cover, below the lowest threshold in the rules (5%).

Each type has a priority in the expert system. When a plot meets the rules of
several types, it is assigned to the one with the highest priority. Each row of
`cand` is one plot: the type it is assigned to, then the types whose rules it
meets, highest priority first. Plot `CX45` meets the rules of `FB` (beech-fir
montane forest, priority 5) and of its parent type `F` (forest, priority 2), and
is assigned to `FB`:

```{r usage-candidates}
cand[cand$plot_id == "CX45", ]
```

`resy_eval_plot(res, p = "CX45")` shows the species and conditions behind this
assignment. For EUNIS, the header table also needs site data such as the
ecoregion and the country, which `resy_harmonize_eunis()` adds from the plot
coordinates.

RESY accepts these column names, or names standardized to
[Darwin Core](https://dwc.tdwg.org/), a standard set of field names for
biodiversity data. The example data stores species names in `scientificName`.

| Column | Also accepted |
|---|---|
| `PlotObservationID` | `PlotID`, `eventID` |
| `TaxonName` | `scientificName`, or any column set with `species_col` |
| `Cover_Perc` | `organismQuantity`, with an `organismQuantityType` of `"% cover"` |
| `Longitude` | `decimalLongitude` |
| `Latitude` | `decimalLatitude` |
| `Country` | `country` |
| `Altitude (m)` | `Altitude`, or `minimumElevationInMeters` and `maximumElevationInMeters` (their midpoint) |

## :scroll: Vignettes

These vignettes show how to use RESY:

- [Classifying vegetation plots with RESY](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/RESY.html):
  start here to get from a species table to classified plots
- [Get EUNIS habitat types](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/EUNIS.html):
  get additional information to classify EUNIS habitat types to plots with coordinates
- [Get altitude data](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/altitude-vignette.html):
  get the altitude column which some EUNIS rules use
- [Match species names](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/articles/taxonomy.html):
  matching the species names in your data to the names the expert system uses

## :desktop_computer: Functions

These are the main functions:

- `resy_classify()` assigns each plot to a vegetation or habitat type
- `resy_candidates()` lists the assigned and candidate types per plot
- `resy_harmonize_eunis()` adds the site data EUNIS needs (ecoregion, country,
  coast, dunes) from the plot coordinates
  `resy_resolve_taxa()` matches names from other taxonomies to them

An overview of all functions and data is given in the tab
[**Reference**](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/reference/).

## :books: Papers and Links

- Chytrý et al. ([2025](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16895007)): the released
  EUNIS expert system versions on Zenodo (first release 2020)
- Chytrý et al. ([2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12798)): the platform
  [FloraVeg.EU](https://floraveg.eu/habitat/) has the descriptions of every EUNIS
  habitat type 
- Bruelheide et al. ([2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12562)): translates the
  expert system of Chytrý et al. (2020) into R
- Chytrý et al. ([2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)): the expert system
  (ESy) uses vegetation surveys and site data to derive EUNIS habitat types.

## :memo: How to cite

```{r citation, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cit <- citation("RESY")
fence <- function(lang, x) {
  cat("```", lang, "\n", paste(x, collapse = "\n\n"), "\n```\n\n", sep = "")
}
cat(attr(cit, "mheader"), "\n\n", sep = "")
fence("text", format(cit, style = "text"))
cat("BibTeX:\n\n")
fence("bibtex", format(cit, style = "bibtex"))
```
